hops.title: Coronin-1 in mouse macrophages and sympathetic neurons
hops.text: A macrophage can digest a swallowed microbe by fusing the pouch that holds it with a lysosome. In 1999, researchers studying mycobacteria found a host protein, now called Coronin-1, coating the pouches that held live bacteria. In mouse macrophages, Coronin-1 turned out to be needed for calcineurin, a calcium-dependent enzyme, to block that fusion. Fifteen years later, Suo and colleagues guessed that NGF-TrkA signaling endosomes might be protected in much the same way. Without Coronin-1, a larger fraction of lysosomes in the cell body were positive for tagged TrkA, and a downstream survival signal faded sooner after NGF withdrawal.

hops.title: A Swedish family whose NGF works through TrkA but not p75
hops.text: People born without working TrkA have a rare condition called CIPA: they cannot feel pain or sweat normally. A large family in Norrbotten, northern Sweden, carries a different change: one swap in NGF itself, arginine to tryptophan at position 100 of the mature protein (R100W). Family members with two copies lack deep pain in bones and joints, which leads to painless fractures and damaged joints, yet they sweat normally and have typical intellectual ability. In cultured cells, the purified mature mutant NGF still activated TrkA and supported neuron survival but failed to engage p75. NGF's two receptors can do separate jobs, as the punishment model assumes.

hops.afterHeading: Activity: a different variable in a different system
hops.title: Why Botox wears off
hops.text: It seems obvious that a silenced muscle should starve its nerve. Botox says otherwise. Botulinum toxin acts at the same neuromuscular junction as curare, but from the nerve side: it stops acetylcholine release, while curare blocks the muscle's receptors. Treated muscles typically move again over about three to four months. Repeated imaging of mouse terminals showed what happens in between: the silenced terminal grows a network of sprouts that form temporary working synapses, then the original ending recovers and the extra sprouts are removed. This is adult muscle, not an embryo, so it does not settle the curare puzzle, but it shows silence can bring branching rather than retreat.

audio.title: Ant bridges, a shared protein, and how mouse nerve endings recover after botulinum toxin
audio.transcript:
In a developing mouse sympathetic ganglion, neurons compete for a limited supply of nerve growth factor. That sounds simple until you ask how the contest actually picks a winner. Here are three true stories from outside the ganglion that make the logic easier to hold on to.

The first is about ants. In a classic experiment published in nineteen ninety, biologists gave a colony of Argentine ants a bridge with two equal branches, leading from their nest to an empty sandy arena. There was no food, only new ground to explore. At first, ants crossed both branches in similar numbers. You might expect the traffic to stay split. Instead, almost all of it ended up on one branch. As ants walk, they lay down trail pheromone. If each ant chose a branch in direct proportion to the scent, an early lead would have no built-in tendency to grow. The model added the same starting weight to each trail and squared the result, so once enough pheromone built up, a small lead in scent became a bigger lead in choices. Later work measured how individual ants steer toward a stronger scent, and showed in a model that random wobble in that steering could amplify a small lead at a fork as well. That is a similar logic to the one in the N G F model: a lead can grow only when the reward rises faster than the lead.

The second story starts with tuberculosis. A macrophage, an immune cell, can digest a swallowed microbe by joining the pouch that holds it to a lysosome, the cell's digestive compartment. In experiments with live mycobacteria, researchers found that a host protein called Coronin one gathers on that pouch and helps keep it away from lysosomes. In mouse macrophages, Coronin one was needed to switch on calcineurin, a calcium-dependent enzyme, and that is what blocked delivery to the lysosome. In twenty fourteen, neuroscientists who knew that story asked whether sympathetic neurons protect their N G F and Track A signaling endosomes in much the same way. They do use Coronin one. Without it, a larger share of lysosomes in the cell body were positive for tagged Track A, and a downstream survival signal faded sooner after N G F withdrawal. A lung pathogen and a developing nerve cell rely on the same protein, Coronin one, in a similar way.

The third story is about Botox. Most of us would guess that nerves follow a simple use it or lose it rule: quiet a muscle, and the motor nerve feeding it should wither. That is part of why the chick embryo result, where paralysis with curare saved motor neurons, feels so backwards. Botulinum toxin quiets a muscle at the same neuromuscular junction, but from the nerve side. It stops acetylcholine release, while curare blocks the muscle's receptors. Doctors use it for some muscle spasms, for chronic migraine prevention and for frown lines. For frown lines, the effect typically lasts about three to four months before wearing off. Repeated imaging in mouse muscle showed what happens in between. The silenced motor terminal does not wither. It grows a network of new sprouts that form temporary working synapses, until the original ending recovers and the extra sprouts are pruned away. That is adult mouse muscle, a different situation from the curare result in embryos, so it does not settle that puzzle. But it shows that a silenced muscle does not simply abandon its nerve.

The ants show how a small lead can grow. Coronin one shows how a neuron can keep a survival signal going. And the mouse muscle shows how much a quiet connection can change.
